sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
CO2 Reduction Reaction (CO2RR) is an effective route to convert CO2 to value-added
products in energy and environment. In this work, a series of CuSe/g-C3N4 electrodes were synthesized by anchoring hexagonal CuSe nanoplates on g-C3N4 nanosheets and used for electrochemical CO2RR. Among the as-prepared electrodes, 50wt% CuSe on g-C3N4 performed the highest Faradaic efficiency of 85.28% to achieve 1.47 times higher than that of the pure CuSe
NPs at -1.2 V vs. RHE due to the larger specific area provided by the introduction of planar-
structure g-C3N4 NSs and faster electron transfer speed on the interface of CuSe NPs and g-C3N4 NSs. Meanwhile the calculations of density functional theory confirmed the electronic coupling
on the electrodes to form an internal electric field between two materials and electron direction
from g-C3N4 NSs to CuSe NPs. This work created a novel opportunity for optimizing design of electrode materials to enhance the CO selectivity of CO2RR.
.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Nowadays, the anthropic excessive emission of carbon dioxide has triggered worldwide
environmental problems and seriously threatened people’s safety in production and life [1,2].
The artificial conversion of CO2 into high value-added products has been regarded as the most promising strategy to relieve the CO2 level in the atmosphere. Among the numerous approaches, including electrocatalysis [3-6], photocatalysis [7-9], photo-electrocatalysis [10,11], thermal-
catalysis [12,13], the electrocatalytic CO2RR has received extensive attention because of its simpler process and lower energy consumption [14,15]. However, the electrocatalytic CO2RR is still hindered by some obstacles like high overpotential and poor selectivity due to the kinetically
inert nature of CO2 and the competition of hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in aqueous electrolyte [16,17]. Therefore, the design and development of catalytic electrodes with high
Faradaic efficiency, desired product selectivity, and material stability are crucial in the research
of CO2RR at the current stage [18].
Since Hori started to use copper (Cu) as a catalytic electrode, Cu-based catalysts have been
favored in CO2RR to produce various organics [2,19,20] through explorations about the crystal planes [21] and size effects [22] of Cu and Cu compounds, such as copper oxide [23], copper
sulfide [24] and single atom Cu [25]. The selenium solid solution with copper in different atom
ratios (CuSe, Cu3Se2, Cu2Se, Cu5Se4, and Cu2-xSe), as the chalcogenide metal compounds, are typical P-type semiconductor [26,27], where the CuSe exhibits diverse crystalline structures of
monoclinic, tetragonal, cubic and hexagonal phases [26,28] and are widely employed in solar
cells [29], photocatalysis [30] and so on. Han et al. studied Cu1.83Se electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to formic acid with 77.6% Faraday efficiency at -2.1V (vs. Ag/Ag + ) [31].
Recently, two-dimensional (2D) materials, especially Klockmannite-phase CuSe nanoplates
(NPs) [32] have been extensive research on electrocatalysis because of fast electronic
transmission capability and more active sites exposed on their surfaces [33]. However, pure
CuSe NPs tend to aggregate and therefore hamper their plays in the electrocatalytic CO2RR. Although various attempts such as coupling CuSe NPs with other semiconductors were realized,
the product selectivity, Faradaic efficiency, and the electrode lifetime still need improvement to
meet the commercial requirement.
g-C3N4 nanosheets (NSs) have planar morphology with few layers and a large surface area,
which provides better support to load and disperse other solids. At the same time, the amino-
group on the g-C3N4 NSs can also anchor special species [34]. Some strategies for doping and coupling semiconductors in or on the g-C3N4 NSs had been proposed [35] such as SnS2/g-C3N4 and CuxSey/g-C3N4 [30,36]. The Ni-g-C3N4 and Cu-g-C3N4 were used for electrocatalytic reducing CO2 to ethanol and other products [34, 37]. In this paper, we designed a CuSe/g-C3N4 composite composed of Klockmannite CuSe and g-C3N4 NSs, where the CuSe NPs were expected to evenly disperse on the g-C3N4 NSs. In practice, a series of CuSe/g-C3N4 with different CuSe mass percent (10%, 30%, 50%, and 70%, 100%) was employed to evaluate their
electrocatalytic activities in CO2RR. Subsequently, necessary characterizations and density functional theory calculations demonstrated the structure of the CuSe/g-C3N4 and electron transition between the CuSe and the g-C3N4 under a self-formed internal electric field. The electrochemical tests confirmed that the best CuSe/g-C3N4 had larger capacitance and a faster charge transfer rate for improving the electrocatalytic efficiency. Finally, the electrochemical
stability of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 was further investigated and an electrocatalytic mechanism of CO2RR was proposed.
2. Experiment
2.1 Materials
Urea (H2NCONH2, 99.0wt%), anhydrous sodium sulfite (Na2SO3, 97.0wt%), selenium
powder (Se, 99.75wt%), and potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99.5wt%) were purchased from Tianjin Damao Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid disodium salt
(EDTA-2Na, 99wt%) was purchased from Tianjin Third Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. Copper(II)
sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO4·5H2O, 99wt%) was purchased from Tianjin Bodie Chemical Co. Ltd. and sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 96wt%) was purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical
Co., Ltd. Carbon dioxide gas (CO2, purity≥ 99.999wt%) was purchased from Tianjin Huanyu Gas Co., Ltd. All the reagents were analytical grade and used as received without further
purification. The carbon cloth (W0S1009) was purchased from Taiwan Cetech Co., Ltd.
2.2 Preparation of g-C3N4 NSs
g-C3N4 NSs was synthesized following the previous report [38]. Typically, the Urea is
heated to 550 °C in a ceramic crucible for 4 h in air.
2.3 Preparation of CuSe NPs
Na2SeSO3 was synthesized from Se, detailed procedure is described in supplement
information, and CuSe NPs were synthesized according to the previous literature [39]. Generally,
10 mL CuSO4·5H2O solution (0.1 M) and 10 mL EDTA-2Na solution (0.1 M) were added into a 100 mL beaker. After stirring for 30 min, NaOH solution (1 M) was added into the beaker to
adjust pH until 12. Then, 10 mL Na2SeSO3 solution (0.1 M) was added to the mixture with
further stirring. The mixture was transferred to a Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave (100 mL)
at 160 ℃ for 12 h. After naturally cooling down to room temperature, the suspension was
centrifuged at 5000 rpm and the black precipitate was washed with water and EtOH for 3 times,
dried at 60 ℃ for 6 h.
2.4 Preparation of dual 2D CuSe/g-C3N4
The preparation steps for CuSe/g-C3N4 were the same as that of CuSe NPs except for
adding a calcuated amount of g-C3N4. The corresponding CuSe/g-C3N4 was denoted as X% CuSe/g-C3N4 (X=10, 30, 50, 70), in which X% represented the mass percent of CuSe NPs in the composites.
2.5 Material Characterization
The crystalline structures were identified by an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Rigaku
Corporation) equipped with Cu Kα irradiation at a scanning region from 5° to 80°. The crystal
morphology and particle size were collected by the scanning electron microscope (SEM, Merlin
compact). The internal structure and the lattice fringes were obtained by transmission electron
microscopy (TEM, Tecnai G2 SPIRIT TWIN) and high-resolution transmission electron
microscopy (HRTEM, Talos F200X) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer
(EDX, Oxford SDD X-Max). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi)
equipped with a monochromatic Al Kα radiation source was used to analyze the composition and
valence of the element. Fourier Transform Infrared (FT-IR) spectra were recorded on a Bruker
Tensor-27 spectrometer to investigate the functional groups. Raman spectroscopy was performed
on HORIBA JOBIN YOVN at the excitation wavelength of 532 nm with a 1μm laser spot. The
hysteresis loops of nitrogen sorption were measured at 77 K on an ASAP2020M instrument.
2.6 Electrochemical Measurements
All the electrochemical experiments were performed in a three-electrode system of an H-
type electrolytic cell with two compartments separated by an exchange membrane (Nafion 117,
Dupont). The carbon cloth, as a working electrode, was further treated as described in the
method section in the supplementary information. The carbon cloth (1 cm×1 cm) coated with the
as-prepared CuSe/g-C3N4, an Ag/AgCl electrode filled with 1M KCl solution and platinum mesh
(1 cm×1 cm) was used as the working. Reference, and counter electrodes, respectively. The
collected potentials were converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) reference scale
using E(RHE)= E(Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 V + 0.059 V × pH.
In a typical preparation procedure of working electrode, 5 mg of CuSe/g-C3N4 was
dispersed in a solution of 500 μL water, 500 μL ethanol, and 100 μL 5wt% Nafion solution under
sonication for 1 hour to form a pseudo-homogeneous CuSe/g-C3N4 ink, whose 30 μL was dropcasted onto the carbon cloth and dried in air. Before the electrochemical tests, the 0.1 M KHCO3 (70 mL) electrolyte was bubbled with CO2 for at least 30 minutes to remove other residual gas, and all tests were carried out at room temperature and atmospheric pressure. CO2 gas was passed into the H-type electrolytic cell with 20 mL/min and the gaseous products were detected by on-
line gas chromatography (GC-7920). A flame ionization detector (FID) was used to detect CO,
and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) was used to quantify H2. The Faraday efficiency was calculated with the formula in supplementary materials.
The electrocatalytic tests were carried out under the electrochemical workstation (CHI660E)
to control the applied potential. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was
performed at 0.352V with the frequency range from 0.01 Hz to 100 kHz at a voltage amplify of 5
mV. The linear scan voltammetry (LSV) curves were conducted with the scan rate of 20 mV/s
between 0 V to -1.4 V vs. RHE in N2 or CO2-saturated KHCO3 electrolyte. Electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) was assessed by the double-layer capacitance (Cdl), which was determined by measuring the capacitive current density associated with the scan-rate dependence
of cyclic voltammetry (CV) plot. Tafel slope was calculated according to the formula:
η=a+blogj; where η is the overpotential, j is the current density and b is the Tafel slope.
2.7 DFT calculations
Theoretical calculation work is based on DMol3 code [40], including structural optimization
and calculation of electronic properties. The generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the
Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation function is used to describe the exchange
and correlation effects [41,42]. The 2D/2D CuSe/g-C3N4 heterostructure is composed of 2×1 single-layer CuSe supercell and 2×1 multi-layer g-C3N4 supercell, which is constructed based on the CuSe and g-C3N4 crystals provided by the XRD pattern. Among them, the bulk CuSe and gC3N4 belong to the hexagonal crystal system, and their space groups are P63/MMC and P-6M2 respectively [43]. The optimization criteria for these structures are (1) energy tolerance≤1.0×10 -5
Ha, (2) maximum force tolerance of 0.002 Ha/Å, (3) maximum displacement tolerance of 0.005 Å, and (4) SCF tolerance≤1.0×10 -6 eV/atom. The top and side views of the model structure after
structural optimization is shown in Figure 1 (a) and (b). The CuSe/g-C3N4 lattice constant after structural optimization is a=13.143Å, and the lattice mismatch rate is 1.79%. The minimum
distance between the two crystal faces of the stable structure is 3.01 Å, which is similar to the
previously reported heterostructure with g-C3N4 as the base catalyst [44, 45]. To investigate the
thermodynamic stability of CuSe/ g-C3N4, this work uses Binding energy (Eb) to express it, and the calculation formula is as follows: [46, 47]
Eb ECuSe g C3N4 ECuSe Eg C3N4
where ECuSe g-C3N4, ECuSe, and Eg-C3N4 represents the total energy of the CuSe/g-C3N4 hybrid
structure, the CuSe, and the g-C3N4, respectively. The calculated of CuSe/g-C3N4 is -0.925 eV, and it is generally considered that a negative value indicates that the formation of
heterostructures is exothermic. Thus, from the perspective of thermodynamics, the
heterostructure formed by CuSe and g-C3N4 is stable, and there is a strong interaction between the surfaces.
The Gibbs free energy ( G) of each reaction step is defined as the difference between the
free energy of the reaction initiation and termination states, and the general formula is described
as [48]:
G E EZEP T S
where E is the total electronic and ionic energy obtained from Density Functional Theory
(DFT) that, total energies of the catalysts, EZEP , is the change of zero-point energy, T is the temperature of 298.15 K, and S is the entropy change. Zero-point energies and entropies of
electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 intermediates were computed from the vibrational frequencies.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussions
sections.text:
The crystalline structure of CuSe NPs, g-C3N4 NSs, and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 were analyzed
by XRD. As shown in Fig 1(a), the characteristic peaks are at 2θ 26.6°, 28.1°, 31.1°, 46.0°,
50.0°, 56.6° were attributed to the (101), (102), (006), (110), (108), (116) crystal planes of CuSe
NPs according to the hexagonal phase CuSe (JCPDS No.34-0171) [49]. For g-C3N4 NSs, two typical diffraction peaks are at 12.9° and 27.5° ascribed to the (110) and (002) crystal planes
(JCPDS 87-1526) [50], which was corresponding to in-plane structural packing motif and
interplanar layered stacking of aromatic system respectively. Significantly, the patterns of 50%
CuSe/g-C3N4 hybrid exhibited similar characteristic peaks to that of CuSe NPs, which demonstrated that the crystalline structure remained unchanged after introducing g-C3N4. Moreover, the intensity of the diffraction peak was distinctly enhanced due to the higher
The morphology of g-C3N4 NSs, CuSe NPs, and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 was visualized by SEM.
In Fig 2(b), CuSe NPs exhibited a typical uniform hexagonal plate with the size of about 200-
300 nm [49]. Furthermore, g-C3N4 NSs were fluffy two-dimensional nanosheets (Fig S2). It could be seen in Fig 2(a) that CuSe NPs with smaller sizes were spread on g-C3N4 NSs to form closed contact.
Fig 2. SEM images of (a) 50% CuSe/g-C3N4, (b) CuSe NPs.
We also conducted TEM and HRTEM analyses to further explore the microstructure and
distribution of the as-fabricated dual 2D CuSe/g-C3N4. As illustrated in Fig S3, the g-C3N4 NSs presented thin layers with numerous wrinkles while the CuSe NPs exhibited a uniform hexagonal
shape, which was consistent with the SEM images. The TEM image of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 in Fig 3(a) suggested the hexagonal CuSe NPs be tightly attached to the irregular g-C3N4 NSs, which is consistent with SEM results. As shown in Fig 3(b), no obvious lattice fringe was found in the
sheet-like g-C3N4 NSs, while the lattice spacing of loaded nanoplate was scaled as 0.288nm and 0.355nm, which indexed the (006) and (101) lattice planes of CuSe NPs [51]. Furthermore, we
also discovered an intimate interface between CuSe NPs and g-C3N4 NSs. Besides, selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns also demonstrated that the CuSe NPs were in a crystalline
state with a strong connection of (006) and (101) planes. Meanwhile, the existence of amorphous
g-C3N4 NSs directly ascertained that CuSe NPs and g-C3N4 NSs had been successfully combined in 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 (Fig 3c). The elemental mapping image of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 in Fig 3(d-h) provided the coexistence and uniform elemental distribution of C, N, Cu, and Se. The above
consequences indicated that the highly dispersed CuSe NPs on g-C3N4 NSs had been achieved successfully. Besides, the X-ray spectrometer (EDX) images visually verified the coexistence of
the mentioned elements (Fig S4).
To further illustrate the electronic properties on the interface of the CuSe/g-C3N4, we
calculated the Projected Density of State (PDOS) of CuSe, g-C3N4, and CuSe/g-C3N4 are shown in Figure 4 (c), (d), (e). From the PDOS distribution of CuSe/g-C3N4, we can find the PDOS of the four elements C, N, Cu, and Se are hybridized with each other, the original electronic state of
g-C3N4 in the conduction band has moved to the right of the Fermi level, which enhances the electron distribution density at the valence band. The recombination of g-C3N4 coulomb potential [52] is more conducive to electron transport. Therefore, the electronic redistribution induced by
the electronic coupling can significantly increase the conductivity of the CuSe/g-C3N4.
Fig 4. (a) Top view of optimized 50% CuSe/g-C3N4, (b) side view of optimized 50% CuSe/g-C3N4. Orange: selenium, pink: copper, blue: nitrogen, gray: carbon; the PDOS of (c) CuSe NPs, (d) g-C3N4 NSs and (e) 50% CuSe/g-C3N4.
The FT-IR analysis in Fig 5 illustrated several characteristic peaks for pure g-C3N4 at the
range of 1200-1800cm -1 attributing the C-N or C=N stretching vibration in the aromatic CN heterocycles [53]. Meanwhile, the sharp peak located at 810 cm -1 originated from the breathing mode of the s-triazine unit [38]. Besides, the broad peaks from 3000 to 3600 cm -1 was ascribed
to the N-H and O-H stretching mode [54]. For CuSe NPs, two slight peaks located at 1387 and 1627 cm -1
were ascribed to Cu-Se vibration modes. As for the 50% CuSe/g-C3N4, the peaks at
1200-1800cm -1 and 810 cm -1
were consistent with those of the g-C3N4. However, the intensities
of peaks at 3000-3600 cm -1
were weaker than those of the pure g-C3N4 NSs, which verified the
interaction between N-H bond of g-C3N4 NSs and CuSe NPs.
Fig 5. FT-IR spectra of g-C3N4 NSs, CuSe NPs, and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4.
To further investigate the elemental composition and surface chemical valence of the
CuSe/g-C3N4, the XPS survey spectra in Fig S5 confirmed the existence of C, N, Cu, and Se in the 50% CuSe/g-C3N4. The C 1s peaks of the pristine g-C3N4 NSs in Fig 6a could be deconvoluted into three peaks located at 284.8, 286.2, and 288.0 eV which corresponded to the sp 3 C-C adventitious carbon, C-N and N=C-N in the aromatic CN heterocycle, respectively [53].
It could be found that for 50% CuSe/g-C3N4, that three peaks shifted slightly which were located at 284.7, 286.1, and 287.8 eV, respectively. Moreover, the N 1s spectrum of g-C3N4 NSs (Fig 6b) was fitted into four main peaks at 398.0, 398.5, 400.1, and 404.1 eV, which were attributed to
triazine rings (C-N=C), tertiary nitrogen (N-(C)3), heterocyclic amino groups (N-H) and πexcitations, respectively [53,55]. Noteworthily, the binding energy of N 1s in the 50% CuSe/g-
C3N4 was higher due to a decrease in electron density around N atoms by the interfacial inaction
with CuSe NPs. As shown in Fig 6c, the binding energy of CuSe NPs at the Cu 2p region could be divided into four peaks. The peaks located at 934.3 and 954.1 eV were associated with Cu 2+
2p3/2 and 2p1/2, respectively. Meanwhile, the peaks located at 932.1 and 951.9 eV were assigned to Cu + 2p3/2 and 2p 1/2, respectively [56]. The observed Cu + is ascribed to the incomplete reduction reaction of CuSe NPs in the presence of SO3 2- as a reductant [39]. Besides, in the Cu 2p XPS spectra, the binding energy of Cu 2+ slightly decreased and then conversely increased comparing to that of CuSe NPs, which indicated the electron density around Cu + dropped. Furthermore, the ratio of Cu + / Cu 2+
was also added up to 2.82 times of CuSe NPs. It also indicated that the introduction of g-C3N4 increased the Cu + amount and enhanced the electrocatalytic CO2RR performance. Also, the Se 3d peaks of CuSe NPs (Fig 6d) had two main peaks at 54.5 and 55.5 eV corresponding to Se 3d 5/2 and 3d 3/2, which was in accordance with Se 2- [56,57]. Another peak located at 58.9 eV was attributed to Se substance [58], demonstrating that Se was partially transferred to Se 2- . Worth
notable that Se 3d XPS spectra of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 displayed a slight shift towards higher binding energy, indicating the variety in the chemical environment of CuSe NPs. In a word, the
above results not only demonstrated the interaction between CuSe NPs and g-C3N4 NSs but also indicated the increased electron density of CuSe NPs in the dual CuSe/g-C3N4.
Fig 6. High-resolution XPS spectra of (a) C 1s, (b) N 1s of g-C3N4 NSs and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4, (c) Cu 2p, (d) Se 3d of CuSe NPs and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4.
Accordingly, the electron transfer direction of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 was also judged by
theoretical calculation. In Fig 7 we obtain the work function of CuSe NPs and g-C3N4 NSs by calculating the corresponding electrostatic potential as shown in Fig 7(a) and (b). The work
functions of CuSe NPs and g-C3N4 NSs are 5.593 eV and 4.763 eV respectively. The smaller work function of g-C3N4 NSs indicates that the electrons are transferred from the g-C3N4 NSs to the CuSe NPs in the CuSe/g-C3N4 till the same Fermi level is reached [59]. To prove the direction of electron flow, we also calculated the planar-averaged electron density difference
along with Z direction for the 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 and showed it in Fig 7(c) [60,61]. The electrons are gathered on the surface of the CuSe NPs at the interface (yellow), while the surface charge is
consumed and the holes are gathered on the g-C3N4 NSs (cyan). This conclusion is consistent not
only with the result of the work function but also with the above XPS analysis. The self-formed
internal electric field near the interface of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 drives electron flowing from gC3N4 NSs to CuSe NPs.
Fig 7. (a) electrostatic potential of CuSe, (b) electrostatic potential of g-C3N4, (c) Planar-averaged electron density difference along with Z direction for the CuSe/g-C3N4 heterostructure. The yellow area: electron accumulation, the cyan area: electron depletion
The nitrogen sorption was conducted to observe the specific surface area and pore size
distribution of the samples (Fig S6). All the isotherms of CuSe NPs, g-C3N4 NSs and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 were type IV hysteresis loop with mesopore. As illustrated in Table 1, the specific surface area of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 was 26.72 m 2 ·g -1 , which was much higher than those of 3.08 m 2 ·g -1 CuSe NPs. A high specific surface area could supply more discharging sites to ease
electron transfer and promote the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. However, compared with 70.34 m 2 ·g -1 of g-C3N4 NSs, the specific surface area of the 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 was smaller due to the introduction of CuSe NPs. Besides, the average pore diameter of the 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 was 17.92 nm, distinctly bigger than 8.19 nm of CuSe NPs and 14.09 nm of g-C3N4 NSs. The superior pore diameter could benefit both CO2 and product diffusions and finally enhance the electrocatalytic performance.

The spectra of Raman spectroscopy in Fig 8(a) described the sharp peak at 257.3cm -1 in
CuSe NPs to the stretching mode of Cu-Se bond of Klockmannite CuSe NPs [62,63], and the
same peak in 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 demonstrated the existence of CuSe NPs. The several flat bulging peaks were on g-C3N4 NSs due to their amorphous structure. As for g-C3N4 NSs, there is a peak at >1000cm -1
, which corresponds to the vibration mode of g-C3N4. The positions at
1350cm -1 and 1550cm -1 correspond to the vibrations of the D band and G band, respectively, caused by the stretching pattern and breathing pattern at the sp 2 site in aromatic rings. Hence, the
characteristic peaks of g-C3N4 appeared.
Fig 8. (a) Raman spectra of g-C3N4 NSs, CuSe NPs, and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4.，(b) enlarged Raman spectra of gC3N4 NSs.
The LSV test results of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 in both N2- and CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3
electrolyte were shown in Fig 9a, where 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 in CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution showed much higher current density than that in N2-saturated KHCO3 solution to suggest 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 having an excellent electrochemical performance for CO2RR rather than hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). In Fig 9b, both CuSe NPs and g-C3N4 NSs possessed a large current density below -0.8 V, while 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 showed a small onset potential of -0.6 V vs. RHE to imply its performance in CO2RR being maximal. Meanwhile, 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 presented a large total current density of 18.02 mA‧cm-2 at -1.4 V, which was superior to 10.44 mA‧cm-2 of
g-C3N4 NSs and 12.01 mA‧cm -2 of CuSe NPs. By increasing the CuSe NPs amount, the total
current density of CO2 of the CuSe NPs at the range of -1.4 to -1.1 V increased first and then reduced by comparing with the current density of N2 as shown in Fig S8a, where the largest current density of the 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 had the faster electron transport rate and the best electrochemical performance.
Fig 9. LSV curves of (a) 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 in N2 and CO2 atmosphere and (b)g-C3N4 NSs, CuSe NPs and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 in CO2 atmosphere; (c) FE plots of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4, (d) partial current density of CO of g-C3N4 NSs, CuSe NPs and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4.
Furthermore, the GC analysis confirmed that H2 and CO was the main reduction product
and no liquid product was detected by the 1 H NMR spectroscopy (Fig S7). The Faraday
efficiency (Fes) for producing CO and H2 were calculated and showed in Fig 9c over the potential range from -0.6 to -1.4 V, wherewith increasing of the potential, the FE of CO (FECO) increased and reached a maximum of 85.28% at an applied potential of -1.2 V vs. RHE, then
dropped to 58.65% at -1.4V vs. RHE due to the enhancement of the excessive applied potential,
thus, the CO2RR performance was decreased. For comparison, the FECO of the g-C3N4 NSs was much lower over the whole potential range and the maximum FECO value was only 11.4% at - 1.4V vs. RHE because HER primarily occurred (Fig S9b). Moreover, the maximum FECO value
of CuSe NPs was 58.57% at -1.2V vs. RHE (Fig S9a), which was lower than that of the 50%
CuSe/g-C3N4. When the CuSe NPs amount in X% CuSe/g-C3N4 from 10%, FECO raised from 62.47% to maximal 85.28% at -1.2 V and then decreased (Fig S10). In Fig 9d the partial current
density for CO (jCO) increased with the increasing of the applied potential for all the g-C3N4 NSs, CuSe NPs, and 50% CuSe/g-C3N4, only 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 exhibited a higher CO current density of -10.5 mA‧cm-2 at -1.4 V. All in all, the excellent electrocatalytic CO2RR performance of the
50% CuSe/g-C3N4 at lower applied potential, higher FE and jCO of the 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 for electrocatalytic CO2RR is in perspective.
The test of the electrochemically active surface area is determined by the double-layer
capacitance (Cdl). In Fig 10(a), 11.0 mF‧cm -2 of capacitance value Cdl of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 was
larger than 7.6 mF‧cm-2 of CuSe NPs, 6.2 mF‧cm-2 of g-C3N4 NSs, and those of X% CuSe/g-
C3N4 (X=10, 30, 50, and 70) to provide larger effective charge capacity and accelerate electrocatalytic CO2RR. The Cdl of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 has the highest electrochemically active surface area, which provides more catalytic active sites. The CO2 adsorption is more conducive on these catalytic active sites, and the next transformation is performed easily.
In Fig 10(c) the Nyquist plots by EIS measurements showed the charge transfer resistance
(Rct) 6.56 Ω of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 being lower than 16.89 Ω of CuSe NPs and 25.74 Ω of gC3N4 NSs, and the linear slope of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 was significantly higher than those of gC3N4 NSs and CuSe NPs. The Nyquist plots for comparison of different amounts of CuSe in CuSe/g-C3N4 were shown in Fig S14, where the semicircle and Rct value of 50% CuSe /g-C3N4
was smallest. In summary, the 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 possessed the fastest charge transfer rate and the optimal performance in electrocatalytic CO2RR.

The dynamic activity for CO formation was elucidated by Tafel slope in Fig 10(a), where
the Tafel slope of 50% CuSe /g-C3N4 was 85.3±3.7 mV·dec -1 , smaller than 119.1±1.6 mV·dec1 of CuSe NPs and 137.7±8.4 mV·dec-1 of g-C3N4 NSs, indicating that 50% CuSe/g-C3N4
possessed more favorable reaction rate for the generation of CO[64].
The stability of electrocatalytic CO2RR was tested by using the I-t curve in Fig 10(b), where
the current density 11.0 mA·cm -2
of 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 remain stable at -1.2V vs. RHE after 14
hrs. Moreover, XRD patterns of the used 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 were similar to the fresh one, but the peak intensity slightly decreased (Fig S13). Therefore 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 had good electrochemical stability.
DFT calculations were performed to obtain insights about the superior activity of CuSe/g-
C3N4. The calculated Gibbs free-energy along the reaction paths of CO2RR indicate that the
formation of *COOH intermediates is the rate-determining step for CuSe and CuSe/g-C3N4[65]
(Fig 11). The Gibbs free energy difference (ΔG) of generating *COOH over CuSe/g-C3N4 is
0.191 eV, lower than that of CuSe, which implies the formation of *COOH being easier in

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we synthesized a series of dual 2D CuSe/g-C3N4 by hydrothermal method and
found the electrocatalytic CO2RR was enhanced after introducing g-C3N4 nanosheets. The 50% CuSe/g-C3N4 exhibited an optimal catalytic performance due to its 85.28% of Faraday efficiency at -1.2V vs. RHE and larger capacitance value, lower charge transfer resistance, as well as an
inner electron field at the interface directed electron flowing from g-C3N4 NSs to CuSe NPs. In conclusion, the mechanism is found that CO2 is activated on the surface of CuSe NPs and controlled by the activation process.
